links.note: Main cause of the disagreement between father and hunter -- the wounded swan, one holding it as prey and one protecting it. That is 28341's sadaya-nirday dispute, not the shooting itself (28340).
The moral the mother teaches through the story: true justice carries daya, protect the innocent. 28345 is that question; 28346 is only the mechanism of handing Rahul the verdict.
Explains the line 'rakshak par bhakshak ko vaare' -- the exact rakshak-versus-bhakshak weighing 28345 names.
Rahul's view of justice -- the innocent's protector has the right. The content of 28345, not the mother's demand (28346).
'If someone kills an innocent creature, what should we do' restates 28345's question almost word for word.

Asks for a description of the garden's beauty (dew-laden flowers, birds, rippling water) before turning to the swan; the described tableau is 28339's, and the swan's fall is only the turn it leads to.
Why 'nyaay daya ka daani' is the poem's most important line -- the line is 28345's answer; the item is judged on the daya-nirdayta weighing, not on who says it (28344).
Asks for the poet plus an introduction to the kaavya-krti it is collected from; the model answer is almost entirely about Yashodhara, its heroine and title, so 28337 over 28338.
Character of the aakhetak -- hard, selfish, pitiless: the 'nirday' half of the pair 28341 sets against the 'sadaya'.
Meaning of 'nyaay daya ka daani' as a proposition about justice -- 28345.
How the poem draws child psychology; the model answer rests on his repeated pleading for a story and the mother giving in, which is exactly 28336. 28335 would only cover the alternation of speech.
How the poem shows the worth of daya and karuna -- the protect-the-innocent question of 28345, argued through Siddharth's choice rather than through the dispute's procedure (28341).
Explicitly asks the student to judge the hunter's viewpoint and express their own view -- 28347 is that share-your-own-view block. 28345 holds the poem's own answer; here the item wants the reader's.
Which speaker says 'lahraata tha paani, haan-haan yahi kahani' -- a sort-the-statements-by-speaker item, 28344, not character identification (28342).
What fell from above -- the swan; 28340's event.
Who lifted the swan (Gautam Buddha) -- the rescuer party of 28341.
Where the many-coloured flowers had bloomed -- the upvan tableau, 28339.
In what state and from where the swan fell -- pierced by an arrow, from above: 28340 precisely.
Whom Yashodhara asks to decide the dispute -- Rahul. 28346 is the mother handing him the verdict; 28345 is the substance of that verdict.
Who is listening to the story -- Rahul. Identification of the listener among the three characters, 28342, rather than attribution of a quoted line (28344).
Who said 'nyaay daya ka daani' -- attribution of a quoted line, which is 28344's task. The line's meaning would be 28345.
What Yashodhara says to Rahul -- decide this dispute, say on whose side justice falls. That is 28346's device verbatim.
What verdict Rahul reaches -- the protector has the right, the devourer none. The content of the answer, so 28345 rather than 28346.
Who demanded the wounded bird -- the aakhetak; the claim that opens 28341's dispute.
Who was the wounded bird's protector -- Siddharth, the 'rakshi' named in the quoted couplet and the sadaya side of 28341.
Who resolved on hath -- the hunter. This is the hunter's obstinacy inside the dispute, not the son's insistence for a story (28336).
Who protected the bird -- Siddharth; the rescuer of 28341.
Why the father would not hand the swan over -- because he had protected it. The refusal is one side of 28341's dispute.
Who speaks the line 'maan, kah ek kahani' -- attribution of a quoted line, 28344. 28336 would cover the insistence itself; here only the speaker is asked.
What the son is insisting his mother do -- tell a story; 28336's hath, asked as content and not as attribution.
Who speaks 'too hai hathi maandhan mere' -- attribution of a quoted line, 28344.
Asks for the poem's title and the poet's name; 28338 is the only concept about the poet. 28337 covers the source work, which this item does not ask for.
The argument Rahul uses to get a story -- 'you are my grandmother's daughter'. The lever of 28336's hath.
For whom 'hathi' and 'maandhan' are used -- the son. 28336 is the concept that names the mother calling him hathi; 28348 would fit only a word-family item, and this asks about reference.
Glosses 'taat' as father -- a vocabulary item, and 28348 is this chapter's word-work block. 28342 would be right only if it asked which character the taat is.
Which natural image 'jhalmal kar him-bindu jhile the' carries -- dewdrops, part of 28339's dawn-garden tableau.
The boy's reaction is that he keeps saying 'haan maan, yahi kahani' -- the twice-occurring echo lines, which is 28350's point about how the repetition carries the mother-son exchange.

Glosses the phrase 'surabhi manmaani' word by word (surabhi = fragrance, manmaani = spreading at will) -- a word-work item on 28348. 28339 holds the scene the phrase sits in, but the question asks the words' sense.
What the mother told Rahul to do -- make the decision. 28346 exactly.
Glosses 'toone guni kahani' as 'understood the story' -- a phrase-meaning item, so 28348 rather than 28346, which is about the demand for a verdict that this line closes.
Glosses 'nirapradh' as nirdosh -- a vocabulary item on 28348. 28345 uses the word but the question asks only its sense.
What Rahul joined justice to -- daya. The substance of 28345's answer.
Which qualities the passage reveals in Rahul -- fearlessness, love of justice, karuna: all read off his rakshak-side verdict, which is 28345.
Glosses 'aakhetak' as shikari -- a vocabulary item on 28348, not the hunter's role in the dispute (28341).
Who lifted the swan -- the taat; the rescuer side of 28341.
Glosses 'lakshya-siddhi' as attaining one's aim -- a phrase-meaning item on 28348; the hunter's claim of it belongs to 28341, but the question asks the sense.
How the father would have felt on seeing the wounded bird -- karuna, prompting the rescue that makes him 28341's sadaya party.

The difference between hunter and father, answered as bhakshak versus rakshak -- 28341's 'ek sadaya tha aur doosra nirday' pairing. 28345 is the moral question drawn from the pairing, not the pairing itself.
